candidates.comment:
Great tutorial on the LM386. The RC network recommended on the output is called a Zobel network or Boucherot cell. The purpose of this is to modify the speaker impedance at high frequencies so that the amplifier will remain stable across its whole bandwidth. The LM386 can sound surprisingly good when it's set up just right and used within its limits.  
Another interesting point about the LM386 is that it produces more distortion as the supply voltage increases if used with low impedance speakers such as most hifi units. With a 4 Ohm speaker it will perform better with a 5V supply than with higher voltages. This is because the output current it can supply is limited, so a higher supply voltage just introduces more THD without actually giving any more power to the load.

candidates.comment:
LM386 is best suited to 8 ohm, though it's fine with 6. It might start clipping if you turn it the whole way up with 6 ohm speakers. But you can add a resistor after the volume potentiometer to push the input signal voltage a bit further to mitigate this.

The output capacitor and speaker form a high pass filter. With a 8ohm speaker and 1000uF cap the cutoff point is roughly 20hz, which is the highest you want it to be. Lower is better. With 6ohm and 1000uF you get 26hz, which will cut off a more noticeable amount of bass. With 6ohm and 2200uF the cutoff is 9hz which is much better. Excellent calculator if you wanna have a play around - https://www.v-cap.com/coupling-capacitor-calculator.php

hope this helps! :)

Output capacitor should be 1000uf at least to get good bass and better working when placing 2.2 to 4.7uf capacitor value between your stereo to mono converter and LM386 input

A lot of what causes the high frequency oscillation is the impedance mismatch  and a Zobel network fixes that problem.

candidates.comment:
Great tutorial on the LM386. The RC network recommended on the output is called a Zobel network or Boucherot cell. The purpose of this is to modify the speaker impedance at high frequencies so that the amplifier will remain stable across its whole bandwidth. The LM386 can sound surprisingly good when it's set up just right and used within its limits.  
Another interesting point about the LM386 is that it produces more distortion as the supply voltage increases if used with low impedance speakers such as most hifi units. With a 4 Ohm speaker it will perform better with a 5V supply than with higher voltages. This is because the output current it can supply is limited, so a higher supply voltage just introduces more THD without actually giving any more power to the load.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses the LM386 amplifier and speaker settings, but does not directly discuss filter capacitors or power supply noise filtering, which are the main topics of the original description.
candidates.comment:
LM386 is best suited to 8 ohm, though it's fine with 6. It might start clipping if you turn it the whole way up with 6 ohm speakers. But you can add a resistor after the volume potentiometer to push the input signal voltage a bit further to mitigate this.

The output capacitor and speaker form a high pass filter. With a 8ohm speaker and 1000uF cap the cutoff point is roughly 20hz, which is the highest you want it to be. Lower is better. With 6ohm and 1000uF you get 26hz, which will cut off a more noticeable amount of bass. With 6ohm and 2200uF the cutoff is 9hz which is much better. Excellent calculator if you wanna have a play around - https://www.v-cap.com/coupling-capacitor-calculator.php

hope this helps! :)

From the LM386 datasheet:

"To make the LM386 a more versatile amplifier, two pins (1
and 8) are provided for gain control. With pins 1 and 8 open

to 200. Gain control can also be done by capacitively coupling
a resistor (or FET) from pin 1 to ground."

candidates.comment:
LM386 is best suited to 8 ohm, though it's fine with 6. It might start clipping if you turn it the whole way up with 6 ohm speakers. But you can add a resistor after the volume potentiometer to push the input signal voltage a bit further to mitigate this.

The output capacitor and speaker form a high pass filter. With a 8ohm speaker and 1000uF cap the cutoff point is roughly 20hz, which is the highest you want it to be. Lower is better. With 6ohm and 1000uF you get 26hz, which will cut off a more noticeable amount of bass. With 6ohm and 2200uF the cutoff is 9hz which is much better. Excellent calculator if you wanna have a play around - https://www.v-cap.com/coupling-capacitor-calculator.php

hope this helps! :)

candidates.comment: That series resistor capacitor on the output is not really a high pass filter, it is a Zoebel network and what that does is keep the output impedance steady across the audio spectrum by compensating for the different inductance of the speaker coil which is dependent on frequency. They are also very useful to make sure you have a good 8 or 4 ohm impedance at the crossover point of a crossover network.  That is why the resistor is added in series with the capacitor.  A lot of what causes the high frequency oscillation is the impedance mismatch  and a Zobel network fixes that problem.

candidates.comment:
Great tutorial on the LM386. The RC network recommended on the output is called a Zobel network or Boucherot cell. The purpose of this is to modify the speaker impedance at high frequencies so that the amplifier will remain stable across its whole bandwidth. The LM386 can sound surprisingly good when it's set up just right and used within its limits.  
Another interesting point about the LM386 is that it produces more distortion as the supply voltage increases if used with low impedance speakers such as most hifi units. With a 4 Ohm speaker it will perform better with a 5V supply than with higher voltages. This is because the output current it can supply is limited, so a higher supply voltage just introduces more THD without actually giving any more power to the load.

to 200. Gain control can also be done by capacitively coupling
a resistor (or FET) from pin 1 to ground."

candidates.comment: That series resistor capacitor on the output is not really a high pass filter, it is a Zoebel network and what that does is keep the output impedance steady across the audio spectrum by compensating for the different inductance of the speaker coil which is dependent on frequency. They are also very useful to make sure you have a good 8 or 4 ohm impedance at the crossover point of a crossover network.  That is why the resistor is added in series with the capacitor.  A lot of what causes the high frequency oscillation is the impedance mismatch  and a Zobel network fixes that problem.

candidates.comment:
LM386 is best suited to 8 ohm, though it's fine with 6. It might start clipping if you turn it the whole way up with 6 ohm speakers. But you can add a resistor after the volume potentiometer to push the input signal voltage a bit further to mitigate this.

The output capacitor and speaker form a high pass filter. With a 8ohm speaker and 1000uF cap the cutoff point is roughly 20hz, which is the highest you want it to be. Lower is better. With 6ohm and 1000uF you get 26hz, which will cut off a more noticeable amount of bass. With 6ohm and 2200uF the cutoff is 9hz which is much better. Excellent calculator if you wanna have a play around - https://www.v-cap.com/coupling-capacitor-calculator.php

candidates.reason: The comment discusses the output of the LM386 amplifier, mentioning the importance of a Zobel network/Boucherot cell for stability and the impact of supply voltage on distortion and performance.
candidates.comment:
Great tutorial on the LM386. The RC network recommended on the output is called a Zobel network or Boucherot cell. The purpose of this is to modify the speaker impedance at high frequencies so that the amplifier will remain stable across its whole bandwidth. The LM386 can sound surprisingly good when it's set up just right and used within its limits.  
Another interesting point about the LM386 is that it produces more distortion as the supply voltage increases if used with low impedance speakers such as most hifi units. candidates.reason: The comment discusses speaker impedance (8ohm vs 6ohm) and its impact on the circuit's performance, which is directly related to the topic of fixing oscillation issues by adding a capacitor to filter out high-frequency oscillations.
candidates.comment:
LM386 is best suited to 8 ohm, though it's fine with 6. It might start clipping if you turn it the whole way up with 6 ohm speakers. But you can add a resistor after the volume potentiometer to push the input signal voltage a bit further to mitigate this.

The output capacitor and speaker form a high pass filter. With a 8ohm speaker and 1000uF cap the cutoff point is roughly 20hz, which is the highest you want it to be. Lower is better. With 6ohm and 1000uF you get 26hz, which will cut off a more noticeable amount of bass. With 6ohm and 2200uF the cutoff is 9hz which is much better. Excellent calculator if you wanna have a play around - https://www.v-cap.com/coupling-capacitor-calculator.php

hope this helps! :)

candidates.reason: The comment discusses amplifier stability and distortion, but does not mention capacitor filtering for oscillation issues as described in the topic. The topics of speaker impedance and supply voltage effects are not directly related to the original topic.
candidates.comment:
Great tutorial on the LM386. The RC network recommended on the output is called a Zobel network or Boucherot cell. The purpose of this is to modify the speaker impedance at high frequencies so that the amplifier will remain stable across its whole bandwidth. The LM386 can sound surprisingly good when it's set up just right and used within its limits.  
Another interesting point about the LM386 is that it produces more distortion as the supply voltage increases if used with low impedance speakers such as most hifi units. With a 4 Ohm speaker it will perform better with a 5V supply than with higher voltages. This is because the output current it can supply is limited, so a higher supply voltage just introduces more THD without actually giving any more power to the load.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses specific details about the LM386 amplifier, including the Zobel network/output RC network, and its limitations with supply voltage and speaker impedance, which are all relevant to building an amplifier for under $3 as described in the topic.
candidates.comment:
Great tutorial on the LM386. The RC network recommended on the output is called a Zobel network or Boucherot cell. The purpose of this is to modify the speaker impedance at high frequencies so that the amplifier will remain stable across its whole bandwidth. The LM386 can sound surprisingly good when it's set up just right and used within its limits.  
Another interesting point about the LM386 is that it produces more distortion as the supply voltage increases if used with low impedance speakers such as most hifi units. With a 4 Ohm speaker it will perform better with a 5V supply than with higher voltages. This is because the output current it can supply is limited, so a higher supply voltage just introduces more THD without actually giving any more power to the load.

Connect pin 2 to GND with 150 ohm resistor, not directly. It will work better. Put 100uf capacitor in parallel with DC input. There is one in your diagram but we often forget it! And if you want bass booster, connect 333 ceramic capacitor (0.033uf) in series with a 15K resistor, and then connect other pin of 15K resistor to pin 1 LM386, and other pin of ceramic capacitor to pin 5. You can also adjust gain between pins 1 and 8. I usually use LM386 as preamp that can have up to 200 gain!

You need a capacitor in parallel to the power source, even if it is a battery. bypass is not needed (pin 7) and will most likely cause some more troubles.

Output capacitor should be 1000uf at least to get good bass and better working when placing 2.2 to 4.7uf capacitor value between your stereo to mono converter and LM386 input

Replace output filter 10 ohm resistor with 4.7 ohm.

candidates.comment:
From the LM386 datasheet:

"To make the LM386 a more versatile amplifier, two pins (1
and 8) are provided for gain control. With pins 1 and 8 open
the 1.35 kΩ resistor sets the gain at 20 (26 dB). If a capacitor
is put from pin 1 to 8, bypassing the 1.35 kΩ resistor, the
gain will go up to 200 (46 dB). If a resistor is placed in series
with the capacitor, the gain can be set to any value from 20
to 200. Gain control can also be done by capacitively coupling
a resistor (or FET) from pin 1 to ground."

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses amplifier settings (LM386 suitability with different ohm speakers), output capacitor and speaker design, and even mentions a specific online calculator tool for coupling capacitor calculations, all aligning closely with the topic's goal of building an amplifier and exploring electronics resources.
candidates.comment:
LM386 is best suited to 8 ohm, though it's fine with 6. It might start clipping if you turn it the whole way up with 6 ohm speakers. But you can add a resistor after the volume potentiometer to push the input signal voltage a bit further to mitigate this.

The output capacitor and speaker form a high pass filter. With a 8ohm speaker and 1000uF cap the cutoff point is roughly 20hz, which is the highest you want it to be. Lower is better. With 6ohm and 1000uF you get 26hz, which will cut off a more noticeable amount of bass. With 6ohm and 2200uF the cutoff is 9hz which is much better. Excellent calculator if you wanna have a play around - https://www.v-cap.com/coupling-capacitor-calculator.php

hope this helps! :)
